claims.text: The initial alloy is a single-phase solid solution.
The initial alloy has a uniform, homogeneously strain-hardened microstructure.
High-strain-rate or extreme-temperature service causes the single-phase HEA to lose toughness.
Mechanical loading produces localized dislocation pile-ups and deformation-induced nanotwin zones.
Localized dislocation and nanotwin structures act as precursors to microcrack formation and brittle failure.
Intense or dynamic loading disrupts initially uniform strain hardening and creates localized heterogeneous regions.
Localized dislocation clusters, enhanced nanotwinning regions, or compositional fluctuations create stress-concentration sites.
The localized heterogeneous regions have a diminished ability to dissipate energy uniformly through plastic deformation.
Stress concentration and diminished plastic-energy dissipation at heterogeneous regions initiate brittle cracks under further loading.
Samples containing induced microstructural heterogeneities will have lower fracture toughness than the pristine baseline.
Heterogeneous samples will exhibit cleavage facets or microcrack paths rather than ductile dimple fracture.
Heterogeneous samples will show lower tensile strain to failure and earlier crack propagation than the baseline.
The as-cast, unaltered baseline has high toughness because of continuous or uniform strain hardening.
Dislocation activity and deformation-induced nanotwinning can sustain strain hardening and suppress plastic instability in a single-phase CrCoNi alloy.
High strain-rate loading is relevant to protective armor applications.
Ambient and cryogenic temperatures define relevant demanding-service boundaries for the proposed toughness-loss mechanism.
The qualitative causal link between localized microstructural evolution and toughness loss is supported by prior work.
The loading thresholds and magnitude of toughness loss are not yet quantified.
